strengths: Comprehensive empirical study of 20 diverse MoE models (3B-57B) providing valuable comparative analysis
Well-designed metrics (SRP, SCH) with formal mathematical grounding and practical motivations
Actionable architectural insights: MoE-on-every-layer + no-shared-experts correlates with superior local routing consistency
Thorough experimental methodology with domain-wise, layer-wise, and expert-level analysis
Strong empirical validation: 90%+ correlation with real cache algorithms (LRU, LFU), high correlation between proposed metrics
Excellent reproducibility: promised code release, detailed corpus construction, 22,528 deterministic samples, confidence intervals
Interesting finding that local routing consistency can coexist with load balance through domain specialization
Practical implication: cache size ~2x active experts balances effectiveness and efficiency
weaknesses: No end-to-end system validation: paper measures potential but provides no demonstrations that high SRP/SCH translates to actual offloading speedups or outperforms existing systems
SCH metric uses oracle information (knowing future expert needs), which is unrealistic and limits practical applicability
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: why shared experts degrade routing consistency and why domain specialization improves both consistency and load balance remain unexplained

Limited technical novelty: extends established phenomenon (consecutive token expert similarity) from 2-4 tokens to longer segments; domain/vocabulary analysis follows Muennighoff et al. (2025) closely
Evaluation limited to single corpus (RedPajama + downstream) and 512-token sequences; generalization to other domains and longer contexts unclear
Suspiciously high correlation (99.7-99.8%) between SRP and SCH (Table 7) suggests potential metric redundancy without clear justification for using both
Missing comparisons with alternative routing consistency metrics and simpler baselines (e.g., basic token-to-token expert overlap)
Data preprocessing differs by model type (SwitchTransformer: masked LM; NLLB: translation), potentially confounding architecture effects with task effects
Figure 2 crowded and difficult to read; key findings (2x cache size recommendation) insufficiently emphasized in main text

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis across 20 diverse MoE models (3B-57B parameters) with careful ablations and position-invariance analysis
Well-formalized metrics (SRP and SCH) with rigorous mathematical derivations and proofs; clear methodology
Interesting empirical observations linking architectural choices (MoE placement, shared experts) and expert specialization patterns to routing consistency
Strong correlation demonstrated between SRP and SCH metrics and common cache algorithms, validating metric design
Thorough presentation with extensive supplementary analyses; reproducibility commitment via code/data release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core observation (consecutive tokens activate similar experts) is not new; prior work (Eliseev & Mazur 2023, Xue et al. 2024b) already exploited this for caching. Main contribution is metric formalization, which is incremental
Primarily descriptive rather than prescriptive: characterizes existing models but provides limited actionable guidance on designing new MoE architectures or improving offloading systems
Lacks causal validation: observes correlations (e.g., domain specialization ↔ routing consistency, MoE placement ↔ SRP) but provides only speculative explanations without controlled experiments
No validation on actual expert offloading systems: claims about practical benefits are unsupported; unclear if high SRP/SCH actually translates to faster inference or better caching performance

Metric design choices not fully justified: F1 score for SRP is somewhat arbitrary; SCH assumes unrealistic oracle knowledge of future activations; optimal cache size (ρ=2) derived from curve observation rather than principled analysis
Weak causal explanation: why do dense modules (shared experts, skipped layers) reduce consistency? The paper speculates but provides no evidence or ablations

Limited scope: small evaluation corpus (22.5K samples × 512 tokens); unclear generalization to longer contexts; post-training effects under-explored; no investigation of performance correlations on downstream tasks

Overstated claims: abstract claims findings 'pave the way for memory-efficient MoE design' but provides limited concrete design recommendations beyond 'avoid shared experts' and 'use MoE on every layer'
Missing ablations and controlled experiments to validate architectural hypotheses (e.g., what happens to SRP when shared experts are removed from a model?)
Load balance vs. routing consistency trade-off noted in Table 2 but not thoroughly analyzed despite practical importance

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical relevance for deploying MoE models on memory-constrained devices
Rigorously designed complementary metrics: SRP for fine-grained analysis, SCH for practical system alignment, with formal mathematical grounding and proofs
Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 20 models (3B-57B parameters) with diverse architectures, large corpus (22,528 samples, 11 domains), and extensive ablations
Strong metric validation: 99.76% SRP-SCH correlation, 97.52% SCH-LRU algorithm correlation demonstrating practical relevance
Identifies actionable architectural patterns (MoE on every layer, no shared experts) and demonstrates load balance can coexist with routing consistency through domain specialization
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and strong commitment to reproducibility (code and corpus release)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core observation (consecutive expert activation) known from prior work (Jiang et al. 2024, Eliseev & Mazur 2023); contribution is systematization rather than discovery

Recommendations largely validate existing practices: identified architectural patterns already followed by state-of-the-art models (LLaMA-MoE-v2, Mixtral, Qwen3), unclear if insights guide future development
Lack of system-level validation: no implementation of actual expert offloading systems using proposed metrics; no concrete measurements of inference speedup or efficiency gains

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: correlations shown but causation unclear (e.g., do domain-specialized experts cause or result from high consistency?); speculation about dense modules interfering with routing (Section 3.3) not rigorously tested

F1 score choice for SRP lacks deep justification; SCH assumes oracle knowledge of future expert activations that real systems cannot access; segment analysis doesn't account for position embeddings and other routing factors

Analysis limitations: no ablation studies isolating architectural component impacts; post-training invariance (Appendix E.1) interesting but under-explored; missing trade-off analysis (consistency vs. model quality)

Evaluation scope concerns: fixed corpus may not generalize to out-of-distribution inputs; no comparison to simpler baseline metrics; group distinctions based on relatively small SRP differences lacking statistical significance tests

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study of 20 diverse MoE models with well-designed metrics (SRP, SCH) that systematically characterize local routing consistency
Novel metrics are rigorously formalized with formal proofs and show strong correlation (>90%) with practical cache algorithms (LRU, LFU)
Thorough analysis across multiple dimensions: architectural factors, domain specialization, layer-wise patterns, with validation through controlled toy model experiments
Clear presentation with intuitive visualizations and extensive supplementary materials including statistical significance testing and confidence intervals
Identifies important tradeoff between local routing consistency and local load balance, while showing global load balance can coexist with high local routing consistency
weaknesses: Critical gap between proposed metrics and practical utility: Appendix F reports weak correlation (r≈-0.3) between local routing consistency and actual throughput on decoding, undermining practical relevance

Limited novelty in insights: findings are mostly confirmatory (load-balance tradeoff, shared experts harm consistency, domain specialization matters) rather than surprising or providing novel understanding
Lack of actionable recommendations: paper characterizes models but doesn't guide practitioners on how to use metrics for design decisions or propose new architectural innovations
Oracle information in SCH definition assumes knowledge of future activations within segment m, which is claimed to be easier to predict than precise timing but not empirically validated

Validation at limited scale: toy models are only 1.43B parameters; unclear generalization to 50B+ models where findings may differ; segment analysis assumes independence between segments ignoring long-range dependencies
